label: Extrinsic Analysis on Manifolds
notes: This chapter, on printed pages 36 through 56, develops the extrinsic program: embed a manifold into Euclidean space, do ordinary statistics there, and project the answer back. We motivate why this is computationally cheap and statistically tractable compared to fully intrinsic methods, and preview consistency and the central limit theorem.

label: The Extrinsic Idea
notes: We start with the guiding picture. A manifold sits as a curved surface inside a high-dimensional Euclidean space through an embedding. Distances are measured by ambient chords rather than along the surface, which turns hard manifold averaging into Euclidean averaging followed by a single projection step back onto the image.

label: Choosing an Embedding
notes: Here we make the embedding concrete. The map j must be a smooth injective immersion onto its image. A good embedding is equivariant under the relevant symmetry group, so that the induced statistics transform correctly. We give the sphere and the Veronese-Whitney embedding of shape spaces as motivating examples.

label: Extrinsic Distance
notes: This slide defines the extrinsic distance as the chordal Euclidean distance between embedded points. Because it is inherited from the ambient norm, it is easy to compute and compare. We contrast it briefly with the intrinsic geodesic distance and note when the two give similar local geometry.

label: The Euclidean Mean Lives Off the Manifold
notes: We emphasize a crucial subtlety. Averaging embedded data in the ambient space produces a point that almost never lies on the image of the manifold. That off-surface mean is the raw material; the projection in the next slides is what restores a valid manifold-valued estimate from it.

label: Nearest-Point Projection
notes: Here we introduce the projection map P that sends an ambient point to its nearest point on the embedded manifold. When the minimizer is unique the projection is well defined and smooth. We set up the variational definition and stress that uniqueness is exactly the nonfocal condition discussed next.

label: Nonfocal vs Focal Points
notes: This slide draws the key distinction. A nonfocal point has a single nearest neighbor on the manifold, so projection is unambiguous; a focal point is equidistant from several, making the nearest point set-valued. The extrinsic mean is defined precisely when the Euclidean mean is nonfocal, guaranteeing a unique projection.

label: The Extrinsic Mean
notes: We assemble the definition. The extrinsic mean is the projection of the ambient expectation of the embedded distribution onto the manifold image, pulled back through the embedding. We state existence and uniqueness under nonfocality and define the sample version by replacing the expectation with the empirical average.

label: Strong Consistency
notes: This slide states the law of large numbers for the estimator. As sample size grows, the embedded sample mean converges almost surely to the embedded population mean; continuity of the projection at a nonfocal point then forces the extrinsic sample mean to converge almost surely to the extrinsic population mean.

label: Central Limit Theorem
notes: Here we linearize. The differential of the projection map transports ambient Gaussian fluctuations of the sample mean onto the tangent space of the manifold. The result is asymptotic normality of the extrinsic sample mean, with a covariance built from the projected ambient covariance restricted to tangent directions.

label: Two-Sample Tests
notes: We apply the theory. To compare two populations we test equality of their extrinsic means using the tangent-space coordinates of the difference and the asymptotic covariances from the central limit theorem. This yields a chi-squared statistic that powers shape-comparison and bootstrap procedures used throughout the book.

label: Recap and Outlook
notes: We close by consolidating the pipeline: embed, average, project, linearize, test. Extrinsic analysis trades a little geometric fidelity for closed-form estimators and clean limit theory. The next chapter contrasts this with intrinsic Frechet means, where averaging happens along geodesics rather than ambient chords.
